Issued at 221 AM EDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Today-Tonight...The center of high pressure over the CONUS 
gravitates towards the Central Plains, while extending across much
of the South Central and Southeastern US, far enough north that 
weak disturbances will be able to transit Florida and the Gulf on 
the southern flank. At the surface, the ridge axis of the Bermuda 
high has set up station north of the Florida peninsula where it 
will remain for the rest of the week, keeping us in onshore 
(easterly) flow. While this regime favors quick development of the
Atlantic breeze, and a sea breeze collision with it's associated 
highest daily storm chances on the western side of the peninsula, 
abnormally high moisture (even for late August) and the 
disturbances aloft will support above normal/scattered to numerous
showers and lightning storms through the daytime and nighttime 
hours. Highest chances 50-70% near the typical afternoon-evening 
period, though showers and storms could get going over the
Atlantic waters and near the coast in the morning, which may throw 
off timing for the rest of the day. Forecast also calls for 
lingering 20-40% chances in the overnight, mainly from convection 
developing over the Atlantic waters moving onshore. 

Model soundings show an atmospheric profile somewhere 
between the typical Florida afternoon environment, and the long- 
skinny profiles favorable for heavy rainfall. Instability is a 
little muted compared to previous days (MUCAPE "only" 2,000-3,000 
J/kg and MLCAPE 1,000-2,000 J/kg) due to the early start, high 
cloud cover, and mid-level temperatures on the warm side (around
M6 C), but low-level lapse rates are very steep (around 8 C/km) 
and will support quick updraft development in the boundary layer. 
Some inhibition exists in the form of a bit of dry air between 
700-500mb, but updrafts that are able to punch through this layer 
will benefit from downdraft enhancement on the way back down. 
DCAPE is a little lower than previous days (700-900 J/kg), but 
water loading may be able to make up the difference. Primary storm
threats are forecast to be gusty winds 45-55 mph, with a very low
(less than 2%) chance for isolated damaging winds around 60 mph, 
frequent cloud to ground lightning, and torrential downpours. 
Modest but deep E-SE steering flow should usher most storms and 
heavy showers along, but some may become slow/erratic where 
multiple boundaries interact, and produce quick, locally high 
rainfall amounts of 2-3" leading to minor flooding. There is a low
(up to 5%) chance for amounts over 4" that could produce greater 
flooding impacts. The Weather Prediction Center has outlooked all 
of East Central Florida in a Marginal (level 1 of 4) risk for 
excessive rainfall. While the environment isn't overly favorable 
for hail, some small hail reports were received yesterday 
(Saturday), and the environment is similar enough to keep the 
threat.

As for the rest of the forecast, seasonably hot temperatures with
highs in the U80s-M90s, which combined with the high humidity, 
will result in peak afternoon heat indices in the U90s-M100s, and 
can't rule out one or two spots touching the U100s. HeatRisk 
impacts remain generally Moderate, with a few pockets of Major in 
and around the Orlando Metro Area, and along the southern coast. 

Monday...Overall setup remains largely unchanged from today 
(Sunday), but the environment is forecast to become even more 
saturated. Model soundings trend closer to the long-skinny 
profile, resulting in a little less instability and downdraft 
enhancement from entrainment, but better supporting heavy 
rainfall. Steering flow may also break down Monday afternoon, 
allowing more storms to become slow/erratic and deliver quick +2" 
inches of rainfall that may lead to flooding. The Weather 
Prediction Center has again outlined all of East Central Florida 
in a Marginal (level 1 of 4) risk for excessive rainfall. The very
high moisture will support greater water loading, which could 
still produce wind gusts 40-50 mph in storms and heavy showers. 
Frequent lightning will remain a threat, but small hail will be 
increasingly unlikely. The high moisture could cause a waterspout
or two to develop over the Atlantic waters or near the coast. 
Little change in temperatures, with highs remaining seasonably hot
in the U80s-M90s. Peak afternoon heat indices increase a degree 
or two to the L-M100s, and there remains a low chances for a few 
locations to reach into the U100s. HeatRisk impacts mostly Minor 
to Moderate.
